items.q: Fluctuating confusion, fever, schistocytes, platelets 18 and haemolysis in an adult need which immediate treatment?
o: Emergency plasma exchange for suspected TTP
items.exp: Suspected TTP (ADAMTS13 failure) kills untreated within days, so plasma exchange (replacing enzyme, removing antibody) starts on clinical suspicion. Platelets are avoided unless bleeding because they may fuel microthrombi.
r: Incorrect. Platelets may worsen microthrombosis in TTP.
Correct. Exchange plasma immediately for suspected TTP.
Incorrect. Splenectomy belongs to refractory immune cytopenias later.
Incorrect. Iron does not treat shearing haemolysis.
items.kp: Schistocytes plus low platelets plus confusion: exchange now, confirm later.

items.q: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes TTP by failing to cleave what?
o: Ultra large von Willebrand factor multimers
items.exp: Without ADAMTS13, ultra large vWF multimers persist, spontaneously agglutinating platelets in microvessels. Autoantibody usually inhibits the enzyme in acquired adult TTP.
r: Incorrect. Fibrinogen is thrombin substrate, not this enzyme target.
Correct. Uncleaved big vWF clumps platelets.
Incorrect. C5 blockade treats complement HUS and PNH.
Incorrect. The enzyme cleaves vWF, not platelets.
items.kp: Big von Willebrand plus no scissors equals TTP.

items.q: A child develops haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and dialysis needing renal failure a week after bloody diarrhoea. Diagnosis?
items.exp: Shiga toxin (E coli O157) injures renal endothelium causing typical HUS with renal dominant microangiopathy after bloody diarrhoea in children. Antibiotics and antimotility agents are avoided in suspected Shiga infection.
r: Incorrect. TTP favours adults with neurology dominance.
Correct. Post diarrhoea renal HUS in a child.
Incorrect. Immune haemolysis lacks this renal diarrhoea sequence.
Incorrect. Spherocytosis crisis lacks thrombocytopenia renal failure.
items.kp: Bloody diarrhoea then failing kidneys in a child equals HUS.

items.q: Atypical HUS without diarrhoea, recurring and familial, results from dysregulation of which system?
items.exp: Atypical HUS follows uncontrolled alternative complement activation (factor H and related defects) injuring endothelium, responding to terminal complement blockade (eculizumab) unlike typical toxin disease.
r: Incorrect. Factor VIII defects bleed, not microangiopath.
Correct. Complement dysregulation drives atypical HUS.
Incorrect. Glycoprotein defects cause platelet bleeding syndromes.
Incorrect. Haptoglobin falls secondarily in all haemolysis.
items.kp: Recurrent diarrhoea free HUS means complement gone rogue.

items.q: Donath Landsteiner antibody causing haemoglobinuria after cold in a post viral child is described as what type?
o: Biphasic cold binding, warm lysing IgG (paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria)
items.exp: Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria antibody binds red cells in cold peripheries and lyses them via complement on central rewarming (biphasic), classically after viral infections in children and resolving spontaneously.
r: Incorrect. Warm antibodies bind at body temperature persistently.
Correct. Biphasic cold warm lysis defines this antibody.
Incorrect. IgM agglutinins clump rather than biphasically lyse.
Incorrect. Hapten needs drug coating presence.
items.kp: Binds cold, bursts warm: Donath Landsteiner biphasic lysis.

items.q: Methyldopa induced haemolysis mechanism is best classified as what?
o: True drug induced autoantibody continuing briefly after withdrawal
items.exp: Methyldopa alters red cell antigens provoking genuine warm autoantibodies that persist weeks after stopping, mimicking idiopathic warm autoimmune haemolysis. Penicillin hapten needs drug present; quinidine forms immune complexes.
r: Incorrect. Hapten describes penicillin type instead.
Correct. Methyldopa makes true autoantibodies.
Incorrect. Oxidant bursts are metabolic, Coombs negative.
Incorrect. Shearing fragments are schistocytes Coombs negative.
items.kp: Methyldopa teaches the immune system to attack red cells itself.

items.q: Massive intravascular haemolysis with bronze skin and shock in gas gangrene follows which toxin action?
o: Alpha toxin lecithinase destroying red membranes (clostridial sepsis)
items.exp: Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin (lecithinase) hydrolyses membrane phospholipids causing catastrophic intravascular haemolysis with spherocytes, jaundice and shock alongside myonecrosis, needing urgent surgery and antibiotics.
r: Correct. Lecithinase lyses membranes catastrophically.
Incorrect. Shiga injures renal endothelium in HUS pattern.
Incorrect. Fever alone does not lyse massively.
Incorrect. Enterotoxin causes diarrhoeal fluid loss.
items.kp: Gas gangrene plus bronze haemolysis equals alpha toxin emergency.

items.q: Cyclical fevers with haemolysis and ring forms plus tetrads (Maltese cross) inside red cells in an asplenic New England patient suggest what?
items.exp: Babesia microti (Ixodes tick) parasitises red cells with Maltese cross tetrads, haemolysing severely in asplenic or elderly hosts, mimicking malaria without travel. Exchange transfusion rescues heavy parasitaemia.
r: Incorrect. Malaria needs exposure geography and lacks tetrad emphasis.
Correct. Tick plus tetrads plus asplenia means babesiosis.
Incorrect. Bartonella bacilliformis is Andean Oroya fever.
Incorrect. Parvovirus stops production without parasitised cells.
items.kp: Maltese crosses in red cells mean Babesia, especially without a spleen.

items.q: Prosthetic mechanical valve haemolysis shows which film and test pattern?
o: Schistocytes with negative Coombs and raised LDH
items.exp: Turbulent jets across mechanical (especially leaking paravalvular) valves shear red cells into schistocytes with complement independent (Coombs negative) haemolysis tracking valve dysfunction severity.
r: Incorrect. Spheres plus positive Coombs mean immune disease.
Correct. Sheared fragments, negative Coombs: mechanical valve.
Incorrect. Bite cells mean oxidant G6PD bursts.
Incorrect. Targets mean thalassaemia or liver disease.
items.kp: Valve plus fragments equals shear haemolysis. Check for leaks.

items.q: DIC differs from TTP at the bedside laboratory first by what?
o: DIC consumes clotting factors prolonging PT and APTT with low fibrinogen; TTP clotting usually normal
items.exp: DIC is systemic coagulation consuming factors (long PT APTT, low fibrinogen, high D dimer) usually with sepsis or obstetric triggers, while TTP is platelet vWF microthrombosis with near normal clotting. Both shear cells and drop platelets.
r: Incorrect. Schistocytes occur in both microangiopathies.
Correct. Clotting consumption separates DIC from TTP.
Incorrect. Platelets fall in both disorders.
Incorrect. Both are Coombs negative mechanical states.
items.kp: Prolonged clotting plus low fibrinogen favours DIC over TTP.
